newsitem.title: UKRAINE: ATHLETICS-BUBKA PLANS TO COMPETE AT SYDNEY OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BUBKA PLANS TO COMPETE AT SYDNEY OLYMPICS.

text.p: Sergei Bubka, apparently recovered from the long-standing Achilles tendon injury which ruined his Olympics last year, plans to compete at the 2000 Sydney Games.
The 33-year-old Ukrainian has set 35 world records and won gold at each of the five world championships to date.
But, apart from winning the 1988 Seoul title, his career has been marred by a series of disasters.
He was denied the chance to win in Los Angeles in 1984 by the Soviet bloc boycott.
At the 1992 Barcelona Games, Bubka failed to clear a height with each of three opening jumps and was ignominiously eliminated.
And at last year's Atlanta Games, Bubka went through a perfunctory warm-up before the final, then packed his gear and left the Olympic stadium.
''Every Olympic year is very hard for me,'' he said in an interview in his impoverished, home town. ''It's fate. Probably I offended God somehow.''

The injury prevented Bubka competing last month at the Donetsk ''Pole Stars'' event he established eight years ago. Instead he was confined to commentating as Russian Pyotr Bochkaryov won with a leap of 5.80 metres.
Bubka, who travels to Finland once a month for medical checks, dismisses talk of retirement and says he still hopes to raise his world record to 6.20 metres.
''I feel quite good,'' he said. ''I am preparing for the world summer championships in Athens. The old injury doesn't bother me any more.
''I want to jump till 2000. I don't like making forecasts. I am a man of action not of words. But I really want to jump 6.20 metres.''
Frenchman Jean Galfione, who won gold in Atlanta last year, said he believed Bubka had at least one more world record left in him.
Galfione, second in the ''Pole Stars'' competition said: ''He can jump higher.
''But now it is more difficult for him because of his age. Also his body is very fragile and he must be very careful.''
Bubka won his first world title in 1983, the year the sport turned professional, and is now wealthy beyond the dreams of his compatriots, who on average earn less than $100 a month.
He left the former Soviet republic in the early 1990s, taking his wife and two sons to Berlin where he opened a sports school.
Local media reported members of the Russian mafia had demanded regular payment from him while he was in Germany and he hired two bodguards before moving to his present home in Monaco.
Bubka says he will know when it is time to retire.
''There is a limit to everything,'' he said. ''After that I will be an ordinary sportsman -- I will play tennis, soccer and basketball just for fun.
''I enjoy mixing sports and business. My business is varied and it's something I want to do in the future.''
